newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Senior China officials to visit Taiwan despite row.
newsitem.headline: Senior China officials to visit Taiwan despite row.

text.p: A group of senior Chinese officials is scheduled to arrive in Taiwan on Thursday for an eight-day visit in a sign of ease of strained relations between Taipei and Beijing, the Taiwan hosts said on Monday.

The 30-member delegation would include Wang Xiaomin, daughter-in-law of one of China's most influential elders, retired parliament chief and Communist Party politburo member Wan Li, sponsoring Chinese Youth International in Taiwan said.
"We invited them for a visit in order to promote understanding and cultural exchanges between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait," a spokesman for the hosts told Reuters.
He said one of the major goals of his organization, a non-profit private group, was to improve understanding and private exchanges between people on rival sides of the Taiwan Strait.
The spokesman said the group will visit cultural, educational and scientific establishments in Taiwan. They will also exchange views with local scholars and experts.
The spokesman said the members of the delegation was decided by the All-China Youth Federation, which hosted a reciprocal visit by a Taiwan group in August, 1996. He did not elaborate.

Local reports said the daughter-in-law of Wan Li, who is expected to visit Taiwan as an advisor to the delegation, had previously applied to visit several times, but was rejected by Chinese authorities due to sour Taipei-Beijing relations.

Officials of Taiwan's top mainland policy-making body, the Mainland Affairs Council, have said the approval for Wang to visit this time indicated that Beijing had relaxed restrictions on visits by senior mainland officials.
Nineteen months ago, China clamped a freeze on what had been slowly warming unofficial ties with Taiwan, which Beijing has seen as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949.

The strained relations were caused by a controversial visit to the U.S. by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui in June 1995, a trip interpreted by Beijing as an attempt to promote independence of the island.
China has warned that if Taiwan declares independence, it will send forces to attack.
China later staged six war games near Taiwan and suspended semi-official talks between the two in a bid to warn Lee against any pro-independence attampts.

Other visitors will include delegation leader Bayinqolu, a vice president of the All-China youth Federation and a secretary of the Communist Youth League of China, and Cheng Jinzhong, a director of the Taiwan affairs office of the State Council.
